questions.prompt: Relative condition number of f(x)=sqrt(x) at x=9 (3 decimals).

options: 1e16, because the spacing of doubles near 1e16 is 2
1e16 + 1 exactly, because doubles store all integers precisely
an overflow error, because the sum exceeds the largest double
1.0000000000000002e16, since one unit goes into the last digit
questions.explanation: Doubles near 1e16 are 2 apart, so +1 rounds back (ties to even).

questions.prompt: float32 spacing near 20,000 m is 2^-9. Express it in millimetres (3 decimals).
kappa=1e9, double precision machine epsilon 2.22e-16. Roughly how many decimal digits of the answer remain correct (nearest integer)?
A colleague says: 'The residual is 1e-15, so the parameter estimates are accurate to 15 digits.' The best reply is
options: Only float128 arithmetic can verify the accuracy, so the residual proves nothing
Residual and error are always equal, so a 1e-15 residual means a 1e-15 error
The residual is meaningless and should be ignored in favour of the parameter values
Residual measures the algorithm; accuracy of x also depends on the condition number
questions.explanation: Check kappa; error can be kappa times larger than the residual.

questions.prompt: Two nearby voltages 5.0001 V and 5.0000 V each have relative error up to 1e-6. The relative error of their difference is about (in percent, nearest integer).
Which statement distinguishes an unstable algorithm from an ill-conditioned problem?
options: Ill-conditioning is sensitivity of the problem itself; instability is avoidable error added by the algorithm
They are the same thing: a problem is ill-conditioned exactly when an algorithm is unstable on it
Ill-conditioning occurs only for singular matrices; instability occurs only for nearly singular ones
Instability is caused by the user's data; ill-conditioning is caused by the chosen algorithm
questions.explanation: Conditioning belongs to the problem; stability belongs to the algorithm.

questions.prompt: In the normal equations kappa(X^T X) = kappa(X)^2. If kappa(X)=1e5, what is the exponent of kappa(X^T X) (equivalently, roughly how many decimal digits can the normal equations lose)?
Which is the best way to compare two floats a and b in a unit test?
options: assert a == b, using exact binary equality
math.isclose(a, b, rel_tol=1e-9, abs_tol=1e-12)
str(a) == str(b), comparing printed forms
abs(a - b) == 0.0, an exact zero difference
questions.explanation: Use a tolerance scaled to the expected error.

questions.prompt: Summing 10 copies of 0.1 gives 0.9999999999999999. What is the absolute error, in units of 1e-16 (1 decimal)?
You must choose between inv(A)@b and a pivoted solve for a calibration matrix whose condition number you estimate as 1e10. Explain what you would do and how you would report the result.
rubric: Prefers a pivoted solve (or QR/SVD) over forming the inverse.
Reports kappa and expected digits lost, about 6 digits left in double precision.
Suggests a verification such as perturbing the data or comparing with higher precision.

questions.prompt: A float32 odometry accumulator stops changing after the robot has driven far from the origin. Predict the cause and propose two code changes.
rubric: Identifies absorption: increments smaller than half the spacing are rounded away.
Proposes float64 or a local origin / separate accumulator.
Mentions compensated summation or a test with large offsets.

questions.skillLabel: Condition number with respect to the matrix
questions.prompt: Fix x=(1,1)^T and let g(A)=Ax with A=[[1,2],[3,4]]. Perturbations of A are measured in the Frobenius norm, outputs in the 2-norm. Give the relative condition number of g at A (3 decimals).
You add n = 2^20 positive float32 numbers. Compared with a plain sequential loop, pairwise (divide-and-conquer) summation changes the worst-case bound on the error relative to sum|x_i| from
options: about (n-1)u to about u, independent of n, because errors cancel at random
about (n-1)u to about log2(n) u, since each term is added only log2(n) times
about n u to about sqrt(n) u, because the partial sums are halved
about log2(n) u to about (n-1)u, because the recursion adds extra roundings
questions.explanation: In the sequential loop an early term is rounded in each of n-1 additions, giving (n-1)u sum|x_i|. In the pairwise tree with n = 2^m every term passes through exactly m = log2 n additions (induction: combining two halves adds one factor 1+delta), so the bound is log2(n) u sum|x_i|, here 20u instead of about 10^6 u. The worst-case bound does not rely on random cancellation, and the tree has fewer, not more, roundings per term.

questions.prompt: Use a stable identity to evaluate cot(0.3) - cot(0.3 + 1e-12). Give the answer in units of 1e-12 (4 decimals), i.e. the number D with value = D x 1e-12.
questions.explanation: cot x - cot(x+y) = sin(y) / (sin x sin(x+y)), since cos x sin(x+y) - cos(x+y) sin x = sin(y). With x = 0.3 and y = 1e-12, sin(x+y) equals sin(x) to 12 digits and sin^2(0.3) = 0.087332, so the value is 1e-12/0.087332 = 1.14505e-11 = 11.4505 x 1e-12. (The naive subtraction gives 1.14500e-11, relative error 5e-5.)
